content: Good evening. I finally have all three renovation quotes in hand and I've been going back and forth on this all week, so I'd really like to work through it carefully with you tonight if that's okay. This decision feels bigger than I expected it to — signing the lease was exciting, but now I'm actually committing to spending a large chunk of money with a specific contractor, and once construction starts there's no easy reversal. The space is the one we've been discussing: 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, Azabu Heights Building, sixty-four and a half square meters on the ground floor.

Good evening, Kenta. That sense of weight is completely appropriate — contractor selection is one of the most consequential decisions in the entire project lifecycle, arguably more consequential than the lease negotiation itself, because a contractor's competence, communication style, and financial discipline will shape everything that happens between now and opening day. A beautiful concept can be ruined by poor execution, and conversely the right contractor can surface ideas and solutions you hadn't considered. The good news is that you now have concrete proposals to work from rather than abstract impressions. So let's go through each bid methodically. You said you have three quotes — tell me who the firms are and give me the headline numbers first, before we get into the details of what each one proposed.

Right, three bids. The first is from a company called Kenchiku Plus — they're a mid-size general contractor based in Minato-ku, fairly well known for commercial fit-outs. They came in at 9.6 million yen. The second is from Yamamoto Koumuten, which is a smaller specialized firm with a focus on restaurant interiors. The owner is a man named Tetsuo Yamamoto and he came highly recommended by my real estate agent, who has worked with him on several past projects. Their bid came in at 8.2 million yen. The third is Sasaki Design Build — they're the most design-forward of the three, and they've done a few restaurant projects I've seen photos of online that are genuinely impressive visually. They came in at 11.1 million yen. So there's a pretty wide spread.

That is a meaningful spread. You're looking at roughly a 2.9 million yen gap between the lowest bid and the highest, which on a project of this size — a 64.5 square meter restaurant fit-out — represents a very significant percentage difference. Before we go firm by firm, I need to ask two foundational questions. First: what is your actual renovation budget? That context is essential because it immediately tells us who is in the game and who is not. Second: did all three firms bid on an identical set of specifications that you gave them, or did each one interpret the brief somewhat differently? When comparing bids, apples-to-apples alignment matters enormously — a lower bid that cuts scope you actually need is not cheaper, and a higher bid that includes things you didn't ask for isn't necessarily more expensive on the things you do need.

My renovation budget is 8.4 million yen. That's the number I communicated clearly to all three firms upfront, in writing, when I sent them the project brief. I told them it was a hard ceiling and I needed them to come in at or under that figure. So as you can see, Kenchiku Plus is already 1.2 million yen over budget, and Sasaki Design Build is nearly 2.7 million yen over. Yamamoto Koumuten is the only firm that actually came in under the ceiling, at 8.2 million yen. On your second question — they mostly bid on the same core specifications, but each firm exercised different degrees of creative interpretation. Kenchiku Plus followed my original brief very closely, almost to the letter. Sasaki Design Build departed significantly from my brief in two specific areas that we can get into. Yamamoto Koumuten also proposed some changes to the original spec, but their changes stayed within the budget envelope.

That renovation budget figure of 8.4 million yen is actually the most important piece of information in this conversation, because it immediately restructures the analysis. With a hard ceiling stated upfront in writing, Kenchiku Plus and Sasaki Design Build have both demonstrated that they either couldn't or didn't take your constraint seriously. Kenchiku Plus came in 14 percent over budget. Sasaki Design Build came in 32 percent over. These aren't rounding errors — these are fundamental misalignments with the project parameters you gave them. Even if you tried to negotiate either of them down to 8.4 million, you'd be starting from a position of weakness: you'd be asking them to reduce by amounts that force painful scope cuts or margin compression on their side, and that creates its own risks during construction. Yamamoto Koumuten being the only firm to actually honor your constraint is itself a meaningful signal about how they run their business. Let's go through each proposal in detail, though. Start with Kenchiku Plus — what did their proposal actually contain, and what's your read on them beyond the number?

Kenchiku Plus was very professional in their presentation. Thick bound document, detailed line items, every element broken out clearly. From a technical competence standpoint I have no serious concerns — they've done a lot of commercial restaurant fit-outs and their references checked out. But the actual proposal was underwhelming in terms of vision. Their kitchen layout was competent but completely conventional — they essentially replicated my original brief without any creative interpretation at all. The finishes they specified were generic: standard subway tile, off-the-shelf millwork, nothing that would create a strong or distinctive visual identity for the space. They proposed a fairly standard semi-open kitchen with a pass-through counter, which is fine, but it creates no memorable moment for guests when they walk in. The proposal read like something they pull from a template for any restaurant client. I don't have concerns about their execution quality, but I also have zero excitement about working with them. And then, of course, there's the budget problem — 9.6 million yen against a renovation budget of 8.4 million yen is a non-starter unless they can shave 1.2 million off, which feels like asking a lot.

Your read on Kenchiku Plus sounds accurate and I think appropriately skeptical. The combination of uninspired design and budget overage is a double flag. Let's address the budget issue directly: getting a contractor to reduce a bid by 1.2 million yen — roughly 12.5 percent — is not impossible, but it almost always means one of three things: cutting scope you actually wanted, substituting lower-quality materials that will disappoint you later, or compressing their labor margin to a point where they start making corners-cutting decisions on-site that you won't discover until something fails during service. When a contractor comes in over a clearly stated ceiling, it signals either that they didn't take the constraint seriously or that their genuine cost structure can't reach it. Neither scenario is particularly reassuring as the basis for a working relationship. The lack of design ambition compounds this — you'd be paying over budget for a restaurant interior that gives guests no particular reason to take a photograph or return. For a new restaurant in Higashi-Azabu trying to establish an identity, that's a real cost even if it doesn't appear on the invoice. I'd keep Kenchiku Plus as a reserve option in case the preferred firms fall through for some reason, but I wouldn't lead with them. Tell me about Sasaki Design Build — you mentioned they departed from your brief in two significant ways.

Sasaki Design Build produced the most visually stunning proposal of the three, by a significant margin. The renderings were beautiful — polished stone surfaces, warm lighting design, a refined northern Italian aesthetic that genuinely matched the mood I'm trying to create for Ginza Trattoria. Looking at those images, I could actually see the finished restaurant. But they made two major unilateral changes to my brief that I hadn't asked for. First, they completely reconfigured the kitchen layout in a way that would require relocating the main drain line — that's a structurally complex and expensive piece of work that wasn't in my original spec and that they just decided was necessary without consulting me first. Second, they specified imported Italian stone for the bar counter and dining surfaces, which I had not requested — and that stone alone accounts for nearly 800,000 yen of their overage above the 8.4 million yen ceiling I had set. When I pushed back on both of those items in our follow-up meeting, their project manager told me the Italian stone was integral to their design vision and that relocating the drain was 'the right thing to do structurally.' That answer made me genuinely uneasy.

That response from Sasaki Design Build's project manager is a red flag that I'd take very seriously. Let me explain why specifically. When a contractor tells you that an 800,000 yen material upgrade is 'integral to their design vision' — on a project where they've already come in 2.7 million yen over your stated hard ceiling — what they're actually telling you is that their aesthetic preferences take priority over your financial constraints. That is a fundamental misalignment in how they see the client relationship. And when they tell you that an unplanned drain relocation is 'the right thing to do structurally,' without having been asked to assess the structure in the first place, they're inserting their judgment in a way that conveniently expands scope and cost. These are patterns, not one-off miscommunications. Design-forward firms that blend their own creative vision with client work can produce extraordinary results — but they can also be the most difficult contractors to manage under construction pressure, precisely because every scope dispute becomes an argument about artistic integrity rather than a straightforward conversation about what was agreed and what it costs. The 11.1 million yen figure is almost secondary to the attitudinal problem. If you engaged Sasaki Design Build, you'd be entering a relationship where their opening position, before construction even starts, is that they know better than you what your restaurant should look like and what it should cost. That dynamic almost never improves once you're on-site and the contractor has leverage. I'd treat their proposal as a valuable visual reference for the design direction you want to communicate to your chosen contractor, but not as a viable path for this project. Now tell me about Yamamoto Koumuten in detail, because based on what you've said, that's where this decision is actually headed.

You're reading the situation correctly. I've been leaning toward Yamamoto Koumuten since the second site visit, and I want to talk through why I feel good about them but also what gives me some hesitation. The positive case starts with Tetsuo Yamamoto himself. He came to the Higashi-Azabu space twice. The second visit, he brought a junior site manager with him and the two of them spent about two full hours going through the ceiling structure, the existing drainage runs, and the HVAC situation in detail. He knows the Azabu Heights Building — apparently Yamamoto Koumuten had done previous work in the building on a different tenant space, so he was already familiar with the building's infrastructure in ways that a contractor seeing it fresh wouldn't be. He also picked up on something important that I would not have caught on my own. He noticed that the existing electrical panel is undersized for a commercial restaurant kitchen and flagged it early as something we needed to budget for explicitly. And then he made a design recommendation that I found genuinely exciting — he proposed an open kitchen with a brick-faced pizza oven facing dining room as the central visual feature of the space. He said it would anchor the entire dining room, create theater for guests, and give the restaurant a focal point that would photograph well for social media. It's the kind of idea that came from someone who was actually thinking about what this restaurant needs to be, not just executing a generic brief.

Everything you've described about Tetsuo Yamamoto's approach is the profile of an engaged, experienced contractor who invests real intellectual effort in a project before the contract is signed — and that diligence during the proposal phase is one of the most reliable predictors of how a contractor will behave once they're on-site. Let me unpack a few specific things you mentioned, because I think their significance is worth making explicit. The prior experience in Azabu Heights Building is a practically underrated advantage. Building-specific knowledge about drainage routing, structural elements, HVAC paths, and electrical infrastructure means fewer costly surprises mid-construction. When a contractor who doesn't know the building encounters an unexpected condition — a drainage run that doesn't go where the plans suggest, a structural member in an inconvenient location — that becomes a change order that costs you money and time. Tetsuo Yamamoto already knowing the building reduces that risk materially. The electrical panel observation is exactly the kind of thing that can become a 400,000 to 600,000 yen surprise change order if it's discovered after construction starts. The fact that he surfaced it proactively, before the contract, and incorporated it into the budget tells you that his 8.2 million yen number reflects actual understanding of the project rather than a low-ball estimate designed to win the job and expand later. On the design recommendation — the open kitchen with the brick-faced pizza oven facing dining room is a strong concept for northern Italian, both from a guest experience standpoint and an operational one. It creates immediate visual legibility: a guest walks in and within seconds understands the restaurant's identity and cooking philosophy. It also creates the kind of ambient theater — watching dough go into a fire-lit oven — that justifies premium pricing and generates the word-of-mouth that a new restaurant needs in its first months. What did Yamamoto say about where the oven would be sourced, and how that fits within the 8.2 million yen figure?

He was very specific on that point, which I appreciated. He recommended sourcing the wood-fired oven through a supplier called Forno Bravo Japan. He explained that they distribute Italian-manufactured ovens domestically and provide local installation support and service — which matters because if something goes wrong with the oven during the first year of operation, you want someone in Japan who can actually respond. He told me he's worked with Forno Bravo Japan on two previous restaurant projects and has confidence in both the product and their installation team. He walked me through the oven he had in mind — a mid-range model that's appropriate for the volume I'm projecting, neither underpowered nor oversized for the space — and said the installed cost would land somewhere in the range of 1.2 to 1.4 million yen. And critically, that figure is already included within his overall 8.2 million yen bid. He didn't present the oven as a separate line item to be decided later; he had already done the specification work, priced it out with Forno Bravo Japan directly, and built it into the total. He also walked me through the ventilation requirements for the wood-fired oven, the floor load implications given that a masonry oven at that scale is genuinely heavy, and the fire suppression coordination requirements. He clearly knew the product well and had thought through the installation dependencies before our meeting.

That depth of pre-contract homework is genuinely unusual and tells you a great deal about how Yamamoto Koumuten operates. The fact that Tetsuo Yamamoto had already contacted Forno Bravo Japan, selected an appropriate model for your volume, understood the installation requirements, and baked the installed cost into the bid means that his 8.2 million yen number is grounded in real pricing rather than estimates. Contractors who leave equipment specifications vague — who say 'we'll sort out the oven separately' or 'that will depend on what you select' — are essentially carrying placeholder costs in their bids that become change order opportunities later. Yamamoto eliminated that ambiguity upfront, which is a mark of professional discipline. I also want to flag the wood-fired oven question as something worth thinking through carefully on the operational side, because it affects your restaurant in ways beyond the renovation scope. A wood-fired oven is a genuine differentiator — it creates flavor characteristics and visual drama that a gas oven simply cannot replicate, and for northern Italian where wood-roasted meats, focaccia, and pizza are central to the menu, it is authentically appropriate. But it comes with operational commitments. Wood storage requires physical space and a reliable supply chain. Ash management is a daily task that requires trained staff. Temperature regulation in a wood-fired oven is a skill — you can't just turn a dial — so your kitchen team will need either to hire someone who knows the equipment or to train. Fire code compliance for wood-burning equipment in Tokyo is more involved than gas. For a restaurant where the oven is the visual centerpiece and the focal point of the dining experience, I would argue those commitments are worth accepting. But you should staff and plan for them from the beginning rather than discovering them six months into operation. Has Yamamoto discussed any of the building management coordination for fire suppression, and are there any aspects of his proposal that gave you pause?

On fire suppression — he mentioned specifically that the building management coordination is something Yamamoto Koumuten has handled before in Azabu Heights Building, which is reassuring since that's a conversation that apparently requires knowing who to talk to in the building management office. He also included a dedicated commercial hood system in his spec, rated appropriately for the oven output. So the ventilation and suppression side seems well considered. The areas where I have hesitation are two things. First, timeline: Yamamoto Koumuten is estimating fourteen weeks of construction from permit issuance. I've been hoping to open by early October, and depending on how long the permit process takes, that timeline is potentially tight. For comparison, Kenchiku Plus estimated twelve weeks, though obviously they have the budget problem. Sasaki Design Build estimated sixteen weeks. So Yamamoto Koumuten is in the middle. Second, and this is more of a psychological concern than a practical one — Yamamoto Koumuten is a small firm. Tetsuo Yamamoto runs a total team of twelve people. Part of me worries about whether that's enough capacity to execute reliably on a project like this.

Let me address both hesitations directly. On the timeline question: the twelve-week estimate from Kenchiku Plus is almost certainly the least reliable number of the three, and I'd encourage you to discount it. A contractor who came in 1.2 million yen over a clearly stated renovation budget of 8.4 million yen, without creative justification for doing so, is also likely to have been optimistic about timeline in order to present a competitive picture. Contractors who underprice to win work frequently also underestimate duration. The fourteen-week estimate from Yamamoto Koumuten, backed by someone with direct knowledge of Azabu Heights Building's infrastructure and a clear understanding of what the project actually involves — including the wood-fired oven installation, the electrical panel upgrade, and the open kitchen configuration — is almost certainly a more honest number. As for the math: if permits issue in late June, which is achievable if you move quickly on the application, fourteen construction weeks takes you to late September to early October. That is actually quite close to your target opening window. The real variable is permit timing, and that's outside any contractor's control. What I'd recommend is pressing Yamamoto Koumuten specifically on two things: first, what the permit dependencies are and which elements have the longest lead time; second, whether there is meaningful pre-permit work — material procurement, detailed drawings, equipment ordering — that can begin before permit issuance so that the fourteen weeks can start from the strongest possible position. On the team size concern: twelve people for a 64.5 square meter restaurant fit-out is genuinely sufficient capacity, and I'd argue that a small specialized firm where the owner is personally engaged in the project often delivers better outcomes than a larger generalist firm where your job is handed to a junior project manager after the contract is signed. Everything you've described about Tetsuo Yamamoto — the two site visits, the electrical panel catch, the Forno Bravo Japan specification, the open kitchen concept — points to someone who will be personally invested in your project's success. Personal owner engagement is worth more than headcount for a project at this scale. I think you've already made your decision, Kenta. Tell me if I'm wrong.

You're not wrong. I'm going to go with Yamamoto Koumuten. I've been leaning that way since the second site visit, but I wanted to articulate the reasoning carefully so I could feel genuinely confident rather than just going on instinct. The budget fit is obviously the primary factor — they're the only firm that actually came in under my renovation budget of 8.4 million yen, and they did so while proposing more, not less. But what really clinches it is the combination of Tetsuo Yamamoto's personal involvement from the beginning, the fact that Yamamoto Koumuten already knows the Azabu Heights Building, the proactive catch on the electrical panel, the Forno Bravo Japan oven sourcing, and most of all the open kitchen with the brick-faced pizza oven facing dining room — that concept is exactly the restaurant I want to build. That's the image I've had in my mind of what Ginza Trattoria should feel like when you walk in the door. Kenchiku Plus gave me nothing to be excited about. Sasaki Design Build showed me something beautiful on paper but gave me serious doubts about the working relationship. Yamamoto Koumuten showed me both competence and vision, and stayed within the budget doing it. What do I need to do next?

That's a well-reasoned decision and I think it's the right one. Congratulations — this is a significant step forward. Here is what your immediate next steps should look like, ordered by priority. First and most urgently, contact Yamamoto Koumuten this week — ideally within the next two to three days — to communicate your selection and request a formal contract draft. Do not let this drift into next week. Good specialized contractors with strong reputations, especially smaller firms like Yamamoto Koumuten where Tetsuo Yamamoto's own capacity is the limiting resource, get picked up by other projects. Your verbal or written selection will effectively hold his calendar, but formalize it quickly. Second, before you sign the contract, make sure it contains four things explicitly. One: a detailed payment schedule tied to construction milestones rather than calendar dates — you want payments to correspond to verified completed work, not to dates that could slip for any reason. Two: a written scope of work that specifies the open kitchen, the brick-faced pizza oven facing dining room using the Forno Bravo Japan unit with model number confirmed, the electrical panel upgrade, and any other specific elements discussed in your meetings. Three: a change order clause requiring your written approval for any scope or cost change above a threshold — I'd suggest 50,000 yen — so that no surprises accumulate without your explicit authorization. Four: a timeline commitment with a realistic float provision that both sides agree to upfront. Third, notify Kenchiku Plus and Sasaki Design Build promptly. You don't need to explain your reasoning in detail — a professional, courteous decline is sufficient and is the right thing to do, since they invested real time in preparing proposals. It also preserves those relationships in case you ever need them for a future project. Fourth, begin the permit application process as soon as possible in parallel with the contract finalization. Every week saved on permits is a direct week saved on your October opening timeline, and permits in Tokyo for commercial restaurant fit-outs, particularly ones involving a wood-fired oven and ventilation modifications, are not trivial. Ask Yamamoto Koumuten specifically whether they handle permit coordination in-house or use an expediter, and whether their prior experience in Azabu Heights Building has any bearing on that process. This is a genuinely good outcome. You found a contractor who knows your building, respects your budget, proactively surfaced a real problem before the contract was signed, and came with a design vision — the open kitchen and brick-faced pizza oven as the focal point — that serves the restaurant you are actually trying to build. Ginza Trattoria is becoming real.
